title: A Seminar Discussion: Conditionals in Argument

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Nurova
dialogue.text: Today I want us to work through a real policy question using conditionals. The question is: should WKU make social media literacy a compulsory module? Let's build the argument using all four conditional types.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: I'll start with a zero conditional — a general truth. If students don't understand how social media algorithms work, they will be manipulated by them. That's a factual relationship.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Nurova
dialogue.text: Good. But be careful — is that really a zero conditional, or a first? Zero conditional would be: if a student doesn't understand algorithms, they are manipulated. Present tense both clauses. You said "will be" — that's first conditional: a prediction.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: You're right. Let me rephrase: if students lack digital literacy, they are more vulnerable to manipulation. Zero conditional.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: For the first conditional, I'd say: if WKU introduces this module next year, student awareness will improve measurably within one semester. That's a realistic prediction.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Nurova
dialogue.text: Good use of first conditional — a genuine prediction with supporting assumption. Amir, can you add a second conditional?

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: If every university in Kazakhstan were to introduce social media literacy courses simultaneously, the national level of digital awareness would rise significantly. But it's not realistic to expect coordination like that.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Nurova
dialogue.text: Exactly — the second conditional flags the unrealistic scale. What about the past? Zhibek?

dialogue.speaker: Zhibek
dialogue.text: If WKU had introduced this module five years ago, graduates who entered the job market in 2022 would have been better prepared for the disinformation environment they faced.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Nurova
dialogue.text: Third conditional — past condition, past result. And can anyone connect the past to the present?

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: If the module had been introduced earlier, students today would already have a foundation to build on. Now they're starting from zero.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Nurova
dialogue.text: Mixed conditional — past if-clause, present result. That's exactly right. Notice how each conditional type moved the argument forward in a different direction: factual basis, prediction, ideal scenario, historical counterfactual, and present consequence of past failure. Four tools, one argument.

task1Items.question: Rustam's first attempt was actually a first conditional, not zero.
Kamila uses zero conditional when predicting student awareness will improve.
Amir's second conditional flags the unrealistic scale of national coordination.
Zhibek uses third conditional to describe a past condition and a present result.
Kamila's mixed conditional connects a past if-clause with a present result.
Dr. Nurova says the four conditional types moved the argument in the same direction.

questions.text: What was wrong with Rustam's first attempt at zero conditional?
opts: He used "will be" — making it first conditional, not zero
questions.correct: He used "will be" — making it first conditional, not zero
questions.hint: "You said 'will be' — that's first conditional: a prediction." Zero = present simple both clauses. ✅

questions.text: What is Rustam's corrected zero conditional?
opts: "If students lack literacy, they will be manipulated."
"If students lack digital literacy, they are more vulnerable."
"If students had learned X, they would know."
"If students studied this, they'd be better."
questions.correct: "If students lack digital literacy, they are more vulnerable."
questions.hint: Present simple + present simple = zero conditional. "If they lack... they are..." ✅

questions.text: Why does Amir use second conditional for national coordination?
opts: Coordinating all universities simultaneously is unrealistic — hypothetical
questions.correct: Coordinating all universities simultaneously is unrealistic — hypothetical
questions.hint: "It's not realistic to expect coordination like that." Second conditional signals the hypothetical/unrealistic. ✅

questions.text: What tense does Zhibek use in her third conditional?
questions.hint: "If WKU had introduced..." (PP) + "would have been better prepared" (would have + pp). Third conditional. ✅

questions.text: What makes Kamila's final sentence a mixed conditional?
opts: Past if-clause + present result (would already have now)
It uses past perfect in the result
questions.correct: Past if-clause + present result (would already have now)
questions.hint: "If the module HAD BEEN introduced earlier" (past/3rd) + "students today WOULD already HAVE a foundation" (present/2nd). Mixed. ✅

questions.text: According to Dr. Nurova, the four conditionals moved the argument in:
questions.hint: "Four tools, one argument." Each conditional addressed a different aspect: fact, prediction, ideal, past failure, present consequence. ✅

questions.text: The seminar was about grammar rules, not a real policy question.
questions.hint: "I want us to work through a REAL POLICY QUESTION using conditionals." — applied grammar in a real argument. ✅

questions.text: What is the factual basis conditional used by Rustam after correction?
questions.hint: "If students lack digital literacy, they are more vulnerable." Present simple both clauses = zero conditional. ✅

questions.text: "If every university WERE TO introduce courses, awareness WOULD rise." — "were to" signals:
questions.hint: "were to" = emphatic form used in second conditional to stress that the scenario is hypothetical or unlikely. ✅

questions.text: "If the module HAD BEEN introduced earlier, students TODAY WOULD ALREADY HAVE a foundation." — this is:
questions.hint: Past Perfect (had been introduced) = 3rd type if-clause + present result (would have now) = 2nd type result = MIXED. ✅

questions.text: "If WKU introduces this module, student awareness will improve." — First conditional because:
opts: WKU genuinely could introduce it — real future possibility
questions.correct: WKU genuinely could introduce it — real future possibility
questions.hint: First conditional = if + Present Simple + will. Real possibility believed by the speaker. ✅

questions.text: "If WKU ___ this module five years ago, graduates ___ better prepared." (3rd conditional)
questions.hint: Third conditional: "had introduced" (PP) + "would have been" (would have + pp). ✅
